claim: Aureochrome is a new type of blue light photoreceptor discovered in the photosynthetic stramenopile alga Vaucheria frigida.
source: Recently, a new type of blue light photoreceptor termed Aureochrome (Aureo) was discovered in the photosynthetic stramenopile alga Vaucheria frigida that has been suggested to function as blue light-regulated transcription factor.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on Aureochrome discovery

claim: Only Aureo1 was shown to bind DNA in a light-dependent manner among the two originally identified Aureo homologs.
source: Originally, two Aureo homologs, named Aureo 1 and 2, were identified, but only Aureo1 was shown to bind DNA in a light-dependent manner (Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2007

claim: Several Aureochrome orthologs from other stramenopile algae have been identified since the discovery of the first Aureos.
source: Since the discovery of the first Aureos, several orthologs from other stramenopile algae such as Ochromonas danica, Fucus distichus, Saccharina japonica and Phaeodactylum tricornutum have been identified (Ishikawa et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2014; Schellenberger Costa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies identifying orthologs

claim: The diatom P. tricornutum has four genes encoding aureochromes: three orthologs of type 1 (PtAu1a, b and c) and one of type 2.
source: The diatom P. tricornutum has four genes encoding aureochromes: three orthologs of type 1 (PtAu1a, b and c) and one of type 2 (Depauw et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Depauw et al., 2012

claim: PtAu1a is involved in light-dependent mitosis regulation.
source: Only PtAu1a has been functionally characterized so far and is shown to be involved in light-dependent mitosis regulation (Huysman et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Huysman et al., 2013

claim: PtAu1a represses high-light acclimation.
source: Only PtAu1a has been functionally characterized so far and is shown to be involved in light-dependent mitosis regulation (Huysman et al., 2013) and repress high-light acclimation (Schellenberger Costa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schellenberger Costa et al., 2013

claim: Aureos typically consist of an N-terminal domain with unknown function, a basic region leucine zipper (bZIP) DNA-binding domain, and a C-terminal light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) sensing domain.
source: Aureos typically consist of an N-terminal domain with unknown function, a basic region leucine zipper (bZIP) DNA-binding domain, and a C-terminal light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) sensing domain.
evidence: Describes the domain architecture of Aureochromes based on established knowledge

claim: LOV domains are a subgroup of the Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) superfamily that sense blue light using a noncovalently bound flavin cofactor.
source: LOV domains are a subgroup of the Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) superfamily that sense blue light using a noncovalently bound flavin cofactor (Zoltowski and Gardner, 2011; Herrou and Crosson, 2011; Losi and Gartner, 2012; Conrad et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing LOV domain properties

claim: Photon absorption of the flavin results in formation of a flavin-C4(a)-cysteinyl adduct with a conserved cysteine residue.
source: Photon absorption of the flavin results in formation of a flavin-C4(a)-cysteinyl adduct with a conserved cysteine residue (Salomon et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Salomon et al., 2000

claim: The effector-sensor topology observed in Aureos differs from the domain topology found in most other LOV photoreceptors where the sensory LOV domain is located N-terminally to the effector domain.
source: The effector-sensor topology observed in Aureos differs from the domain topology found in most other LOV photoreceptors where the sensory LOV domain is located N-terminally to the effector domain.
evidence: Based on comparison with known LOV protein architectures

claim: DNA binding of Aureos might be influenced by light-induced LOV domain dimerization.
source: Recent biochemical and spectroscopic experiments on V. frigida Aureo1 (VfAu1) and PtAu1a led to the hypothesis that DNA binding of Aureos might be influenced by light-induced LOV domain dimerization and that structural changes of the N– (A´α) and C-terminal (Jα) helices flanking the LOV core play a key role in this process (Toyooka et al., 2011; Herman et al., 2013; Mitra et al., 2012; Herman and Kottke, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies proposing this hypothesis

claim: Structural changes of the N– (A´α) and C-terminal (Jα) helices flanking the LOV core play a key role in light-induced LOV domain dimerization.
source: Recent biochemical and spectroscopic experiments on V. frigida Aureo1 (VfAu1) and PtAu1a led to the hypothesis that DNA binding of Aureos might be influenced by light-induced LOV domain dimerization and that structural changes of the N– (A´α) and C-terminal (Jα) helices flanking the LOV core play a key role in this process (Toyooka et al., 2011; Herman et al., 2013; Mitra et al., 2012; Herman and Kottke, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The crystal structure of the VfAu1 LOV domain showed an unexpected dimeric arrangement.
source: This hypothesis was supported to some extent by the crystal structure of the VfAu1 LOV domain that showed an unexpected dimeric arrangement (Mitra et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitra et al., 2012

claim: The VfAu1 LOV domain structure was determined from crystals grown in the dark.
source: However, this structure was determined from crystals grown in the dark and it remains unclear whether the observed dimeric LOV arrangement represents the biologically relevant light state dimer.
evidence: States the experimental conditions of the prior structural study

claim: Dark adapted LOV domain containing PtAu1a variants show the typical signature of an oxidized flavin mononucleotide (FMN) chromophore with a main absorption maximum at 448 nm.
source: UV-vis spectra of dark adapted LOV domain containing PtAu1a variants show the typical signature of an oxidized flavin mononucleotide (FMN) chromophore with a main absorption maximum at 448 nm and several subsidiary peaks (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by UV-vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Upon light activation, a new absorption maximum appears at 390 nm indicating FMN-cysteine adduct formation.
source: Upon light activation, the intensities of these absorption bands decrease and a new maximum appears at 390 nm indicating FMN-cysteine adduct formation.
evidence: Supported by UV-vis spectroscopy data and known spectral properties of FMN-cysteine adducts

claim: The dark state recovery time constant for PtAu1afull is 826 ± 19 s.
source: For PtAu1afull, PtAu1abZIP-LOV and PtAu1aLOV, time constants of 826 ± 19 s, 811 ± 4 s and 1500 ± 7 s were determined, respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of dark state recovery kinetics

claim: The dark state recovery time constant for PtAu1abZIP-LOV is 811 ± 4 s.
source: For PtAu1afull, PtAu1abZIP-LOV and PtAu1aLOV, time constants of 826 ± 19 s, 811 ± 4 s and 1500 ± 7 s were determined, respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of dark state recovery kinetics

claim: The dark state recovery time constant for PtAu1aLOV is 1500 ± 7 s.
source: For PtAu1afull, PtAu1abZIP-LOV and PtAu1aLOV, time constants of 826 ± 19 s, 811 ± 4 s and 1500 ± 7 s were determined, respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of dark state recovery kinetics

claim: The presence of the bZIP DNA binding domain accelerates the recovery kinetics of the LOV domain about 1.8-fold.
source: For PtAu1afull, PtAu1abZIP-LOV and PtAu1aLOV, time constants of 826 ± 19 s, 811 ± 4 s and 1500 ± 7 s were determined, respectively, indicating that the presence of the bZIP DNA binding domain accelerates the recovery kinetics of the LOV domain about 1.8-fold.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of recovery kinetics data

claim: PtAu1afull has an average molar mass of 55.1 kDa in the dark and 53.3 kDa in the light as measured by MALS.
source: Quantification of the average molar mass of PtAu1afull (Figure 2a) and PtAu1abZIP-LOV (Figure 2b) in the dark and light state yielded similar values of 55.1, 53.3, 31.7 and 33.7 kDa, respectively
evidence: Supported by MALS measurements shown in Figure 2a

claim: PtAu1abZIP-LOV has an average molar mass of 31.7 kDa in the dark and 33.7 kDa in the light as measured by MALS.
source: Quantification of the average molar mass of PtAu1afull (Figure 2a) and PtAu1abZIP-LOV (Figure 2b) in the dark and light state yielded similar values of 55.1, 53.3, 31.7 and 33.7 kDa, respectively
evidence: Supported by MALS measurements shown in Figure 2b

claim: PtAu1afull and PtAu1abZIP-LOV exist in an equilibrium between dimers and monomers irrespective of light conditions.
source: Peak tailing and a continuous decrease of the molar mass signal in the dark and light state of PtAu1afull and PtAu1abZIP-LOV suggested an equilibrium between dimers and monomers irrespective of the light conditions.
evidence: Inferred from MALS data showing peak tailing and molar mass changes

claim: Illumination induces conformational changes in PtAu1afull and PtAu1abZIP-LOV.
source: Illumination-induced small differences in the elution volumes, indicating conformational changes of both protein variants have occurred as also reported for VfAu1 (Toyooka et al., 2011; Hisatomi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by MALS data and citations to similar observations in VfAu1

claim: Light activation of PtAu1aLOV shifts the oligomerization state from monomers to dimers.
source: In contrast to PtAu1afull and PtAu1abZIP-LOV, light activation of PtAu1aLOV shifts the oligomerization state from monomers to dimers (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by MALS measurements shown in Figure 2c

claim: The elution volume of PtAu1aLOV decreases from 16.2 ml in the dark to 15.2 ml in the light.
source: The change in oligomerization state is reflected by a decrease of the elution volume from 16.2 ml (dark) to 15.2 ml (light) and an increase of the calculated average molar mass from 20 kDa (dark) to 28 kDa (light).
evidence: Supported by MALS measurements

claim: The calculated average molar mass of PtAu1aLOV increases from 20 kDa in the dark to 28 kDa in the light.
source: The change in oligomerization state is reflected by a decrease of the elution volume from 16.2 ml (dark) to 15.2 ml (light) and an increase of the calculated average molar mass from 20 kDa (dark) to 28 kDa (light).
evidence: Supported by MALS measurements

claim: The Kd for the monomer-dimer transition of dark-adapted PtAu1aLOV is 13.6 ± 1.4 µM.
source: Quantification of the monomer–dimer transition using microscale thermophoresis (MST) revealed a Kd of 13.6 ± 1.4 µM for the dark adapted protein (Figure 2d)
evidence: Supported by MST measurements shown in Figure 2d

claim: Pre-illumination of PtAu1aLOV increases its dimerization ability.
source: pre-illumination of PtAu1aLOV increased the dimerization ability as expected from the MALS measurements (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by MST measurements

claim: PtAu1a does not possess cysteine residues outside the LOV domain.
source: We did not observe such light-dependent oligomerization in our experiments and can also rule out an influence of the redox potential on the oligomerization state of PtAu1a, as PtAu1a does not possess cysteine residues outside the LOV domain.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of PtAu1a

claim: The EC50 of PtAu1afull for DNA binding in the dark is 860 nM.
source: Semi-quantitative data evaluation using the Hill equation revealed an effective concentration for 50% response (EC50) of 860 nM in the dark and a Hill coefficient of 1.35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3 and quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The EC50 of PtAu1afull for DNA binding in the light is 90 nM.
source: Illumination with blue light results in a decrease of the EC50 to 90 nM (Hill coefficient of 1.65)
evidence: Supported by EMSA data

claim: PtAu1afull has a 9.6-fold higher affinity for DNA in its light compared with its dark state.
source: Illumination with blue light results in a decrease of the EC50 to 90 nM (Hill coefficient of 1.65), revealing a 9.6-fold higher affinity of PtAu1afull to DNA in its light compared with its dark state.
evidence: Calculated from EC50 values obtained from EMSA data

claim: PtAu1afull displays sequence-specific DNA binding.
source: In the dark as well as light experiments, PtAu1afull displayed no or only weak binding to the DNA probe lacking the target sequence, confirming sequence-specific DNA binding of PtAu1afull.
evidence: Supported by EMSA experiments with DNA lacking the target sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)

claim: The presence of MgCl2 in EMSA experiments is essential for PtAu1afull sequence specificity.
source: The presence of MgCl2 in the EMSA experiments is essential for PtAu1afull sequence specificity, as also described for other bZIP transcription factors (Moll, 2002).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and citation to Moll, 2002

claim: In the absence of MgCl2, sequence specificity and light-dependence of DNA binding are negligible.
source: In the absence of MgCl2, sequence specificity and light-dependence of DNA binding are negligible (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The PtAu1aLOV dark state structure reveals a LOV monomer that adopts a typical PAS fold consisting of a five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet flanked by several helices.
source: The dark state structure revealed a LOV monomer that adopts a typical PAS fold consisting of a five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet flanked by several helices.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The LOV core of PtAu1aLOV closely resembles the structure of VfAu1 LOV with an r.m.s.d between 0.42 and 0.58 Å for 101 Cα atoms.
source: The LOV core forms the chromophore binding pocket and closely resembles the structure of VfAu1 LOV (Mitra et al., 2012) (root-mean-square deviation (r.m.s.d) between 0.42 and 0.58 Å for 101 Cα atoms and molecules A and B PtAu1a and A,B,C,D,E,F for VfAu1a).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with VfAu1 LOV structure

claim: The LOV core is flanked at the N- and C-termini by prominent α-helical extensions denoted A´α and Jα, respectively.
source: The LOV core is flanked at the N- and C-termini by prominent α-helical extensions denoted A´α and Jα, respectively.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The C-terminal Jα helix partially folds back onto the surface of the β-sheet and interacts with the LOV core via hydrogen bonds.
source: As observed for VfAu1 LOV (Mitra et al., 2012), the C-terminal Jα helix partially folds back onto the surface of the β-sheet and interacts with the LOV core via hydrogen bonds between the conserved residue Gln365 and the carbonyl and amine group of Cys316 as well as the side chains of Tyr357 and Gln330.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data and comparison with VfAu1 LOV

claim: A´α forms an amphipathic three-turn helix.
source: A´α forms an amphipathic three-turn helix and interacts with the LOV core through a highly conserved 4 amino acid linker with Ala248, Glu249, Glu250 and Gln251 in the hinge region.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: A´α folds back across the surface of the β-sheet and covers a large hydrophobic patch in the dark state.
source: In addition to Jα, A´α also folds back across the surface of the β-sheet and covers a large hydrophobic patch (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4c

claim: The chromophore binding pocket is mainly formed by hydrophobic residues that stabilize the FMN chromophore together with Gln350, Gln291, Asn319, Asn329.
source: The chromophore binding pocket is mainly formed by hydrophobic residues that stabilize the FMN chromophore together with Gln350, Gln291, Asn319, Asn329, which form hydrogen bonds with the heteroatoms of the isoalloxazine ring.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: FMN is stabilized by Arg304 and Arg288, which interact with the phosphate group of the ribityl chain.
source: FMN is additionally stabilized by Arg304 and Arg288, which interact with the phosphate group of the ribityl chain.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The conserved photoreactive Cys287 is located in the Eα helix on the opposite site of the core β-sheet.
source: The conserved photoreactive Cys287, which forms a covalent bond with FMN upon illumination, is located in the Eα helix on the opposite site of the core β-sheet.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: Blue light illumination induces formation of a parallel PtAu1aLOV dimer.
source: (b) Blue light illumination induces formation of a parallel PtAu1aLOV dimer.
evidence: Supported by light state crystal structure shown in Figure 4b

claim: Illumination results in a release of A'α from the LOV β-sheet and exposes the dimerization site.
source: (d) Illumination results in a release of A'α from the LOV β-sheet and exposes the dimerization site.
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures shown in Figure 4d

claim: Light-activated PtAu1aLOV crystallized as a dimer that features an assembly similar to other N-cap-comprising PAS dimers.
source: As expected from the MALS measurements, light-activated PtAu1aLOV crystallized as a dimer that features an assembly similar to other N-cap-comprising PAS dimers (Figure 4b) (Heintz et al., 2014; Ayers and Moffat, 2008).
evidence: Supported by light state crystal structure and citations to similar PAS dimer structures

claim: The observed parallel dimer arrangement differs significantly from the antiparallel dimer arrangement observed for the dark state structure of VfAu1 LOV.
source: The observed parallel dimer arrangement differs significantly from the antiparallel dimer arrangement observed for the dark state structure of VfAu1 LOV (Mitra et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison with VfAu1 LOV structure

claim: The buried surface area of the PtAu1aLOV light state dimer is 1524 Å2.
source: Analysis of the contact area using the PISA web server revealed a buried surface area (BSA) of 1524 Å2, which is similar to that observed for the VIVID light state dimer (1342 Å2), supporting the observed dimer arrangement as biologically relevant.
evidence: Supported by PISA analysis of crystal structure data

claim: The main dimerization interface is formed by a network of hydrophobic residues on the core β-sheet and A´α.
source: The main dimerization interface is formed by a network of hydrophobic residues on the core β-sheet and A´α.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The C-terminal part of Jα is unstructured in the light state.
source: Compared with the dark state structure, the C-terminal part of Jα is unstructured and the hydrogen bonds between Gln365 and the carbonyl and amine group of Cys316 are broken, indicating light-induced Jα undocking from the LOV β-sheet and subsequent unfolding as suggested previously (Herman et al., 2013) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by light state crystal structure data

claim: The hydrogen bonds between Gln365 and the carbonyl and amine group of Cys316 are broken upon illumination.
source: Compared with the dark state structure, the C-terminal part of Jα is unstructured and the hydrogen bonds between Gln365 and the carbonyl and amine group of Cys316 are broken, indicating light-induced Jα undocking from the LOV β-sheet and subsequent unfolding as suggested previously (Herman et al., 2013) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures

claim: The side chains of Cys316 and Leu317 undergo conformational changes upon illumination.
source: Interestingly, the side chains of Cys316 and Leu317 located on strand Gβ also undergo conformational changes upon illumination, which may promote light-induced Jα undocking from the LOV core.
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures

claim: Jα contributes directly to the stability of the light state dimer by interacting with A'α of the second protomer.
source: Jα seems to contribute directly to the stability of the light state dimer by interacting with A'α of the second protomer.
evidence: Inferred from light state crystal structure

claim: The formation of the covalent Cys287–FMN adduct and the resulting doming of the isoalloxazine ring at position C4a are supported by the Fo-Fc omit map and the 2Fo-Fc map.
source: The formation of the covalent Cys287–FMN adduct and the resulting doming of the isoalloxazine ring at position C4a are supported by the Fo-Fc omit map and the 2Fo-Fc map (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron density maps from crystal structure data

claim: Light-induced rotamer changes were observed for Leu317, Phe331, Ile333, Cys351, and Met313.
source: Light-induced rotamer changes were observed for a variety of residues predominantly in the vicinity of the FMN cofactor (Leu317, Phe331 and Ile333) or on the outer side of strand Iβ (Cys 351) and Gβ (Met 313).
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures

claim: The highly conserved Tyr266 shows a light-induced rotation out of the dimer interface, which is prerequisite for LOV dimerization.
source: Additionally, the highly conserved Tyr266 located on strand Bβ shows a light-induced rotation out of the dimer interface, which is prerequisite for LOV dimerization.
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures

claim: HDX-MS measurements on PtAu1aLOV revealed slightly reduced deuterium incorporation into fast-exchanging amides of A´α in light-adapted PtAu1aLOV.
source: Measurements on PtAu1aLOV confirmed the important role of A´α for dimer formation and revealed slightly reduced deuterium incorporation into fast-exchanging amides of A´α in light-adapted PtAu1aLOV (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Decreased conformational dynamics is observed for helix Eα encompassing the photoreactive cysteine upon illumination.
source: Decreased conformational dynamics is observed for helix Eα encompassing the photoreactive cysteine that forms the covalent Cys287-FMN adduct upon illumination.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: Structural stabilization is observed for the end of strand Hβ with its adjacent loop upon illumination.
source: Structural stabilization is observed for the end of strand Hβ with its adjacent loop that is in hydrogen bonding distance to Bβ upon dimer formation.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: Only negligible light-induced differences in deuterium uptake are observed for Jα.
source: Only negligible light-induced differences in deuterium uptake are observed for Jα that was shown to unwind upon illumination (Herman et al., 2013) and that is also partially unstructured in the light state crystal structure.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data and comparison with prior studies

claim: Jα is highly dynamic already in the dark.
source: This originates from the fact that Jα is highly dynamic already in the dark and amide hydrogen exchange is too rapid to detect a further light-induced increase of the hydrogen exchange rate of Jα due to the limited time resolution of the chosen HDX-MS approach.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS data and known limitations of the technique

claim: A´α is highly dynamic and shows a high degree of deuterium incorporation in the dark and light.
source: In addition to Jα, A´α is also highly dynamic and shows a high degree of deuterium incorporation in the dark and light (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4f

claim: The moderate protection observed for the crystallographic PtAu1aLOV light state dimer interface upon illumination suggests a rapid monomer–dimer interconversion.
source: The moderate protection observed for the crystallographic PtAu1aLOV light state dimer interface upon illumination is in line with HDX-MS measurements performed on VIVID (Lee et al., 2014) and suggests a rapid monomer–dimer interconversion.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS data and comparison with VIVID

claim: HDX-MS measurements on PtAu1afull revealed pronounced destabilization of several elements of the LOV domain upon illumination including Jα and A´α.
source: In contrast to the weak light-induced changes observed for PtAu1aLOV, measurements on PtAu1afull revealed pronounced destabilization of several elements of the LOV domain upon illumination including Jα and A´α (Figure 5a–c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5

claim: Elements within the bZIP DNA-binding domain are significantly destabilized upon illumination.
source: Additionally, elements within the bZIP DNA-binding domain are significantly destabilized, whereas the N-terminal domain and bZIP–LOV linker region are mainly unaffected by LOV activation.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: The N-terminal domain and bZIP–LOV linker region are mainly unaffected by LOV activation.
source: Additionally, elements within the bZIP DNA-binding domain are significantly destabilized, whereas the N-terminal domain and bZIP–LOV linker region are mainly unaffected by LOV activation.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: The deuterium exchange behavior of LOV domain peptides of light-activated PtAu1afull and free PtAu1aLOV are nearly identical.
source: The deuterium exchange behavior determined for LOV domain peptides of light-activated PtAu1afull and free PtAu1aLOV are nearly identical, indicating no differences in the conformation or interaction state of the free or effector-coupled LOV domain in the light state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The pronounced differences in deuterium exchange of the LOV and bZIP domains between dark- and light-adapted protein can be explained by a direct interaction between the two domains in the dark.
source: Therefore, the pronounced differences in deuterium exchange of the LOV and bZIP domains between dark- and light-adapted protein can be explained by a direct interaction between the two domains in the dark, which is broken upon illumination and subsequent LOV dimerization.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS data

claim: The N-terminal part of the leucine zipper is the potential interaction site of the LOV and bZIP domains in the dark.
source: Closer inspection of the HDX-MS data suggests the N-terminal part of the leucine zipper as the potential interaction site of the two domains in the dark.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS data showing bimodal exchange behavior

claim: Peptides within the N-terminal part of the leucine zipper revealed bimodal exchange behavior, indicative of two distinct protein populations with slow interconversion.
source: Peptides within this region revealed bimodal exchange behavior, indicative of two distinct protein populations with slow interconversion and significantly different deuterium exchange kinetics (EX1 kinetics (Konermann, Pan, and Liu, 2011)), which might reflect bZIP–LOV dissociation during labeling (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5d

claim: The N-terminal domain as well as the linker connecting the bZIP and LOV domain are highly dynamic and probably unstructured.
source: The N-terminal domain as well as the linker connecting the bZIP and LOV domain show rapid deuterium uptake in the dark and light, which identifies these regions as highly dynamic and probably unstructured as also suggested from secondary structure prediction (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data and secondary structure prediction

claim: Subtle light-induced structural destabilization was observed for the region between residues 28 and 44 of the N-terminal domain.
source: Subtle light-induced structural destabilization was observed for the region between residues 28 and 44 of the N-terminal domain, which suggests that illumination also affects the function of the N-terminal domain.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: Illumination results in an increased DNA binding affinity of PtAu1afull, reflected by a pronounced protection of the basic DNA binding region.
source: As expected from the EMSA experiments, illumination results in an increased DNA binding affinity of PtAu1afull, reflected by a pronounced protection of the basic DNA binding region and a decrease in structural dynamics of leucine zipper peptides (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data in the presence of DNA

claim: DNA binding and illumination affect not only the bZIP domain but also several elements within the LOV domain, indicating bidirectional allosteric signaling.
source: DNA binding and illumination not only affect the bZIP domain but also several elements within the LOV domain, indicating bidirectional allosteric signaling as also reported for the blue light-regulated phosphodiesterase 1 (BlrP1) of Klebsiella pneumoniae (Winkler et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data and comparison with BlrP1

claim: The presence of DNA in the dark measurements induces similar effects within the LOV domain as illumination in the absence of DNA, suggesting DNA-induced bZIP–LOV dissociation.
source: Interestingly, the presence of DNA in the dark measurements induces similar effects within the LOV domain as illumination in the absence of DNA, suggesting DNA-induced bZIP–LOV dissociation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: The N-terminal domain of PtAu1afull does not show significant differences in deuterium incorporation in the presence of DNA and seems to play a negligible role for light-dependent DNA binding.
source: The N-terminal domain of PtAu1afull does not show significant differences in deuterium incorporation in the presence of DNA and seems to play a negligible role for light-dependent DNA binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: PtAu1aLOV and PtAu1abZIP interact in the dark.
source: We obtained an independent confirmation of the suggested bZIP–LOV interaction in the dark from MALS experiments. We incubated PtAu1aLOV together with PtAu1abZIP upon which the elution volume shifted to a lower volume and the molar mass signal increased slightly compared with PtAu1aLOV alone (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by MALS data shown in Figure 6

claim: Light-induced increase of Rg was observed for PtAu1afull in SAXS measurements without DNA.
source: Estimation of the radius of gyration (Rg) using the Guinier approximation was possible and revealed a light-induced increase of Rg in the measurements without DNA (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by SAXS data

claim: PtAu1abZIP-LOV exhibited a slight increase in the Rg and the maximum particle diameter (Dmax) upon illumination, indicating light-induced protein elongation.
source: As observed for PtAu1afull, PtAu1abZIP-LOV also exhibited a slight increase in the Rg and the maximum particle diameter (Dmax) upon illumination, indicating light-induced protein elongation (Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by SAXS data

claim: Rigid body modeling of the PtAu1abZIP-LOV dark state shows the LOV monomers arranged close to the potential bZIP–LOV interaction site identified by HDX-MS.
source: Rigid body modeling of the PtAu1abZIP-LOV dark state shows the LOV monomers arranged close to the potential bZIP–LOV interaction site identified by HDX-MS and confirms an interaction of the LOV domain with the leucine zipper in the dark (Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by SAXS-based rigid body modeling shown in Figure 7a

claim: Illumination together with DNA binding induces bZIP–LOV dissociation and results in an elongated protein–DNA complex.
source: However, light measurements of PtAu1abZIP-LOV in the presence of DNA clearly show that illumination together with DNA binding induces bZIP–LOV dissociation and results in an elongated protein–DNA complex with Rg and Dmax values that are significantly larger than those observed for dark-adapted PtAu1abZIP-LOV (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by SAXS data and shape reconstruction shown in Figure 7b

claim: In the dark, A'α covers the hydrophobic dimerization site of the LOV β-sheet that becomes exposed upon illumination and thus enables LOV dimerization.
source: In the dark, A'α covers the hydrophobic dimerization site of the LOV β-sheet that becomes exposed upon illumination and thus enables LOV dimerization.
evidence: Supported by comparison of dark and light state crystal structures

claim: Jα undocks from the LOV β-sheet and partially unfolds upon illumination.
source: However, not only A'α, but also Jα is affected by blue light illumination. It undocks from the LOV β-sheet and partially unfolds.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The light-induced structural changes observed for A'α and Jα are in line with Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy studies.
source: The light-induced structural changes observed for A'α and Jα are in line with Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy studies that also indicate light-induced structural changes in both helices (Herman and Kottke, 2015; Herman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by comparison with FT-IR studies

claim: A'α is only affected by illumination in the presence and after unfolding of Jα.
source: Interestingly, it was reported that A'α is only affected by illumination in the presence and after unfolding of Jα, whereas Jα unfolds even in the absence of A'α (Herman and Kottke, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herman and Kottke, 2015

claim: Allosteric signaling between A'α and Jα occurs via the LOV β-sheet and involves the central strand Iβ.
source: Since a direct interaction between the two helices is not observed in the dark state PtAu1aLOV crystal structure, the interdependence between A'α and Jα indicates an allosteric interplay between the two helices as suggested previously (Herman and Kottke, 2015). Allosteric signaling occurs via the LOV β-sheet and involves the central strand Iβ, which is covalently coupled to Jα and also interacts with A'α in the dark.
evidence: Inferred from crystal structure data and prior studies

claim: A combination of light-induced structural rearrangements within the LOV core together with undocking of Jα from the β-sheet are required to trigger the release of A'α from the LOV core.
source: Since the dimer arrangement observed in the PtAu1aLOV light state structure differs from the dimeric assembly observed in the recently determined dark state crystal structure of VfAu1 LOV (Mitra et al., 2012), it can be concluded that a combination of light-induced structural rearrangements within the LOV core together with undocking of Jα from the β-sheet are required to trigger the release of A'α from the LOV core, which ultimately induces the formation of the biologically relevant light state dimer.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of PtAu1a and VfAu1 structures

claim: A'α and Jα of phototropin-LOV2 exhibit structural changes independently of each other.
source: In contrast to the consecutive structural changes reported for the flanking helices of PtAu1a LOV, A'α and Jα of phototropin-LOV2 exhibit structural changes independently of each other (Zayner et al., 2012; Takeda et al., 2013), which implies differences in the signaling mechanism of Aureos and Phototropins.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on phototropin-LOV2

claim: The LOV domain directly interacts with the leucine zipper region of the bZIP domain in the dark, impeding its DNA binding function.
source: Instead, our data suggests a mechanism where the LOV domain directly interacts with the leucine zipper region of the bZIP domain in the dark, impeding its DNA binding function.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS, SAXS, and functional data

claim: Upon blue light illumination, structural changes occur within the LOV core that are transmitted to the flanking helices and result in bZIP–LOV dissociation and subsequent LOV dimerization.
source: Upon blue light illumination, structural changes occur within the LOV core that are transmitted to the flanking helices and result in bZIP–LOV dissociation and subsequent LOV dimerization, thus increasing the affinity of PtAu1a for its target DNA sequence (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by integration of structural, HDX-MS, SAXS, and functional data; model shown in Figure 8

claim: Blue light illumination increases the affinity of PtAu1a for its target DNA sequence.
source: Upon blue light illumination, structural changes occur within the LOV core that are transmitted to the flanking helices and result in bZIP–LOV dissociation and subsequent LOV dimerization, thus increasing the affinity of PtAu1a for its target DNA sequence (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data and mechanistic model

claim: The allosteric signaling mechanism explains the absence of changes in structural dynamics of the bZIP–LOV linker region upon illumination.
source: Such an allosteric signaling mechanism not only explains the absence of changes in structural dynamics of the bZIP–LOV linker region upon illumination, but also explains the need for the > 30 amino acids long linker in Aureos, which is required to enable direct bZIP–LOV interaction.
evidence: Inferred from HDX-MS data and structural considerations

claim: The > 30 amino acids long linker in Aureos is required to enable direct bZIP–LOV interaction.
source: Such an allosteric signaling mechanism not only explains the absence of changes in structural dynamics of the bZIP–LOV linker region upon illumination, but also explains the need for the > 30 amino acids long linker in Aureos, which is required to enable direct bZIP–LOV interaction.
evidence: Inferred from structural and functional data

claim: Recent data on N-terminally truncated and modified VfAu1 constructs indicate an interaction between the leucine zipper and the LOV domain in the dark.
source: Our model is further supported by recent data on N-terminally truncated and modified VfAu1 constructs that also indicate an interaction between the leucine zipper and the LOV domain in the dark, although it was hypothesized that this interaction stabilizes the monomeric form of the synthetic proteins (Nakatani and Hisatomi, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakatani and Hisatomi, 2015

claim: A mechanism involving light-induced release of the LOV domain from its interaction site on the bZIP domain is consistent with the general concept of LOV and PAS domain signaling via the β-sheet surface.
source: Moreover, a mechanism involving light-induced release of the LOV domain from its interaction site on the bZIP domain is consistent with the general concept of LOV and PAS domain signaling via the β-sheet surface (Harper et al., 2003; Zoltowski et al., 2007; Möglich et al., 2009; Nash et al., 2011; Rivera-Cancel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on LOV and PAS domain signaling

claim: The concerted undocking of A'α, Jα as well as of the bZIP domain from the LOV core can be used for the design of new optogenetic tools.
source: In addition to their dimerization ability, the concerted undocking of A'α, Jα as well as of the bZIP domain from the LOV core can be used for the design of new optogenetic tools.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential applications

claim: The light-sensitive bZIP–LOV interaction observed in Aureos allows combining the engineering strategies developed for leucine zippers and coiled coils with the light-sensing function of LOV domains.
source: The light-sensitive bZIP–LOV interaction observed in Aureos allows combining the engineering strategies developed for leucine zippers and coiled coils with the light-sensing function of LOV domains.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential applications

claim: This unique combination of different functionalities provided by Aureos offers new design strategies for robust and tightly controllable molecular switches.
source: This unique combination of different functionalities provided by Aureos offers new design strategies for robust and tightly controllable molecular switches that allow precise spatial and temporal control of biological processes.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential applications

claim: Aureochrome LOV domains have been successfully applied in engineered light-activatable synthetic transcription factors and receptor tyrosine kinases based on light-dependent homo-dimerization.
source: In fact, our data also explain the underlying working mechanism of recently engineered Aureo LOV containing light-activatable synthetic transcription factors and receptor tyrosine kinases that are based on light-dependent homo-dimerization (Yang et al., 2013; Grusch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013 and Grusch et al., 2014

claim: Colorless PtAu1aLOV crystals obtained under blue light illumination are indicative of formation of the flavin-C4(a)-cysteinyl adduct.
source: To obtain the structure of a fully light-adapted PtAu1aLOV dimer, we set up crystallization screens of wildtype PtAu1aLOV under continuous blue light illumination and obtained colorless crystals overnight. Their lack of color is indicative of formation of the flavin-C4(a)-cysteinyl adduct.
evidence: Inferred from known spectral properties of FMN-cysteine adducts
